newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Herzog warns against danger of prejudice. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Germany's Herzog warns against danger of prejudice. [CORRECTED 23:00 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects day of opening of Year against Racism).
By Emma Thomasson

German President Roman Herzog on Sunday warned against prejudice and called on citizens to be more brotherly towards one another ahead of the German opening of the European Year against Racism on Tuesday.

"People must recognise that negative images of others are dangerous fictions which must be put aside through patient education," Herzog told the launch of an annual week set up to improve relations between Germany's Christians and Jews.
Herzog is due to speak at the German opening of the European Year against Racism in Berlin on Tuesday aimed at "pulling up the roots of racism and xenophobia".

The Year, which has a budget of 4.7 million European currency units ($5.55 million), was officially opened in the Netherlands in January, as the European Union vowed to fight racial discrimination, xenophobia and anti-Semitism.
Herzog said although Germany should be thankful it was not plagued by terrorism or civil war, it still had its problems.
"It is still doubtful whether a climate of real brotherliness prevails here," Herzog said.

Germany suffered a wave of racist violence following unification in 1990, particularly in the economically backward, formerly communist east of the country and commentators fear economic problems are leading to a new surge of racism.
Der Spiegel weekly magazine said the danger of a new wave of right-wing extremism was "a ticking timebomb".
Thousands of neo-Nazi skinheads clashed with left-wing activists in Munich on Saturday as they demonstrated against an exhibitions on crimes committed by Hitler's Wehrmacht army.
Record unemployment of 4.66 million in January, not seen since Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933, has sparked accusations that foreigners have stolen jobs from Germans.

Mainstream politicians had long refrained from directly linking the high unemployment level to the country's eight million foreign residents, in part because they wanted to avoid being accused of fomenting racial unrest.
But in January Finance Minister Theo Waigel said it was "grotesque" that millions of Germans were unemployed while so many foreigners were working here.

"Everyone knows that argument is rubbish," retorted Anetta Kahnet, spokeswoman of a working group against xenophobia in the states of former East Germay. "Germans do not want the jobs foreigners take."
Berlin's Tagesspiegel said the Brandenburg representative of foreigners, Almuth Berger, had compiled a report showing a "very open and direct" rise in xenophobia in the state which surrounds Berlin.
Berger said rising unemployment was prompting racist attacks on a new target -- people from other EU countries working in Germany.
Campaigners say a new law which obliges foreign children to apply for residence permits to remain in the country will not help the problem.

Under the rule which came into force last month, children under 16 from Turkey, Tunisia, Morocco and former Yugoslavia now have to apply for visas to visit relatives in Germany and those living here already must obtain a residence permit.
The 2.2 million members of Germany's Turkish community do not have German citizenship, meaning their children now have to apply as "foreigners" for permits.
"This new law just helps the arguments of right-wing extremists," Khanet said. "We need to respond constructively, not destructively to our social problems."
